entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 5 Eze 5:1-17 . Vision of Cutting the Hairs, and the Calamities Foreshadowed Thereby. 1. knife ... razor-- the sword of the foe (compare Is 7:20 ). This vision implies even severer judgments than the Egyptian afflictions foreshadowed in the former, for their guilt was greater than that of their forefathers. thine head-- as representative of the Jews. The whole hair being shaven off was significant of severe and humiliating ( 2Sa 10:4 , 5 ) treatment. Especially in the case of a priest; for priests ( Le 21:5 ) were forbidden "to make baldness on their head," their hair being the token of consecration; hereby it was intimated that the ceremonial must give place to the moral. balances-- implying the just discrimination with which Jehovah weighs out the portion of punishment "divided," that is, allotted to each: the "hairs" are the Jews: the divine scales do not allow even one hair to escape accurate weighing (compare Mt 10:30 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11020"/><div sID="gen19851" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11020"/>2. Three classes are described. The sword was to destroy one third of the people; famine and plague another third ("fire" in <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.2">Eze 5:2</reference> being explained in <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.12">Eze 5:12</reference> to mean pestilence and famine); that which remained was to be scattered among the nations. A few only of the last portion were to escape, symbolized by the hairs bound in Ezekiel's skirts (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.3">Eze 5:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.40.6">Jr 40:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.16">52:16</reference>). Even of these some were to be thrown into the fiery ordeal again (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.4">Eze 5:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.41.1">Jr 41:1</reference>, 2, &c.; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.14">Jr 44:14</reference>, &c.). The "skirts" being able to contain but few express that extreme limit to which God's goodness can reach. <div eID="gen19851" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11021"/><div sID="gen19852" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11021"/>5-6. Explanation of the symbols:<div eID="gen19852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jerusalem--</hi>not the mere city, but the people of Israel generally, of which it was the center and representative.<div eID="gen19853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19854" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... midst--</hi>Jerusalem is regarded in God's point of view as center of the whole earth, designed to radiate the true light over the nations in all directions. Compare Margin ("navel"), <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.12">Eze 38:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.48.2">Psa 48:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">Jr 3:17</reference>. No center in the ancient heathen world could have been selected more fitted than Canaan to be a vantage ground, whence the people of God might have acted with success upon the heathenism of the world. It lay midway between the oldest and most civilized states, Egypt and Ethiopia on one side, and Babylon, Nineveh, and India on the other, and afterwards Persia, Greece, and Rome. The Phoenician mariners were close by, through whom they might have transmitted the true religion to the remotest lands; and all around the Ishmaelites, the great inland traders in South Asia and North Africa. Israel was thus placed, not for its own selfish good, but to be the spiritual benefactor of the whole world. Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.67.1-Ps.67.7">Psa 67:1-7</reference> throughout. Failing in this, and falling into idolatry, its guilt was far worse than that of the heathen; not that Israel literally went beyond the heathen in abominable idolatries. But "corruptio optimi pessima"; the perversion of that which in itself is the best is worse than the perversion of that which is less perfect: is in fact the worst of all kinds of perversion. Therefore their punishment was the severest. So the position of the Christian professing Church now, if it be not a light to the heathen world, its condemnation will be sorer than theirs (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.13">Mt 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.11.21-Matt.11.24">11:21-24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.28">He 10:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.29">29</reference>). <div eID="gen19854" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11023"/><div sID="gen19856" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11023"/><hi type="bold">7. multiplied--</hi>rather, "have been more abundantly outrageous"; literally, "to tumultuate"; to have an extravagant rage for idols.<div eID="gen19856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19857" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither have done according to the judgments of the nations--</hi>have not been as tenacious of the true religion as the nations have been of the false. The heathen "changed" not their gods, but the Jews changed Jehovah for idols (see <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.6">Eze 5:6</reference>, "changed My judgments into wickedness," that is, idolatry, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.11">Jr 2:11</reference>). The Chaldean version and the Masora support the negative. Others omit it (as it is omitted in <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.12">Eze 11:12</reference>), and translate, "but have done according to the judgments," &c. However, both <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.12">Eze 11:12</reference> and also this verse are true. They in one sense "did according to the heathen," namely, in all that was bad; in another, namely, in that which was good, zeal for religion, they did not. <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.9">Eze 5:9</reference> also proves the negative to be genuine; because in changing their religion, they have not done as the nations which have not changed theirs, "I (also) will do in thee that which I have not done." <div eID="gen19857" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11025"/><div sID="gen19859" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11025"/>9. See on <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.7">Eze 5:7</reference>.<div eID="gen19859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19860" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that which I have not done--</hi>worse than any former judgments (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.6">La 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.12">Da 9:12</reference>). The prophecy includes the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, and the final one by Antichrist (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.8">Zec 13:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.2">14:2</reference>), as well as that by Nebuchadnezzar. Their doom of evil was not exhausted by the Chaldean conquest. There was to be a germinating evil in their destiny, because there would be, as the Lord foresaw, a germinating evil in their character. As God connected Himself peculiarly with Israel, so there was to be a peculiar manifestation of God's wrath against sin in their case [Fairbairn]. The higher the privileges the greater the punishment in the case of abuse of them. When God's greatest favor, the gospel, was given, and was abused by them, then "the wrath was to come on them to the uttermost" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.16">1Th 2:16</reference>). <div eID="gen19860" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11027"/><div sID="gen19862" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11027"/><hi type="bold">11. as I live--</hi>the most solemn of oaths, pledging the self-existence of God for the certainty of the event.<div eID="gen19862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19863" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">defiled my sanctuary--</hi>the climax of Jewish guilt: their defiling Jehovah's temple by introducing idols.<div eID="gen19863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19864" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">diminish--</hi>literally, "withdraw," namely, Mine "eye" (which presently follows), that is, My favors; <reference osisRef="Job.36.7">Job 36:7</reference> uses the Hebrew verb in the same way. As the Jews had withdrawn from God's sanctuary its sacredness by "defiling" it, so God withdraws His countenance from them. The significance of the expression lies in the allusion to <reference osisRef="Deut.4.2">De 4:2</reference>, "Ye shall not diminish aught from the word which I command you"; they had done so, therefore God diminishes them. The reading found in six manuscripts, "I will cut thee off," is not so good. <div eID="gen19864" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11028"/><div sID="gen19865" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11028"/>12. Statement in plain terms of what was intended by the symbols (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.2">Eze 5:2</reference>; see <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.12">Eze 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.15.2">Jr 15:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.21.9">21:9</reference>).<div eID="gen19865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19866" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">draw out ... sword after them--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Lev.26.33">Le 26:33</reference>). Skeptics object; no such thing happened under Zedekiah, as is here foretold; namely, that a third part of the nation should die by pestilence, a third part by the sword, and a third be scattered unto all winds, and a sword sent after them. But the prophecy is not restricted to Zedekiah's time. It includes all that Israel suffered, or was still to suffer, for their sins, especially those committed at that period (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.21">Eze 17:21</reference>). It only received its primary fulfilment under Zedekiah: numbers then died by the pestilence and by the sword; and numbers were scattered in all quarters and not carried to Babylonia alone, as the objectors assert (compare <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.4">Ezr 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.3.8">Es 3:8</reference>; Ob 14).<div eID="gen19866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19867" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pestilence ... and famine--</hi>signified by the symbol "fire" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.2">Eze 5:2</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.13.8">Is 13:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.5.10">La 5:10</reference>; plague and famine burning and withering the countenance, as fire does. <div eID="gen19867" type="x-p"/>
